# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

My hands have found three kinds of parts: a display, a light, and three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3. Every state reads unknown to me — touch alone gives me no colours, no printed markings, nothing more than the parts themselves. And my only possible action is a cut, which is irreversible and fatal if wrong. So cutting now would be pure gambling. I will not touch the cut lever until I know exactly which wire the manual wants.

The circuit I need to build is clear: I can only talk to Mute. Mute reads the manual and can hear me, but Mute cannot see the bomb. Deaf can see the bomb but arrives after me each round, and Deaf can never hear me at all — Deaf only gets my gestures, and I only get Deaf's spoken words at the start of the next round. So Mute is my bridge: I report what I feel, Mute checks the manual and gestures my questions to Deaf, and Deaf speaks the visuals back to both of us. This round I seed that loop: give Mute my full tactile inventory and ask for the manual's rules, and wave to Deaf just to announce I'm here and active.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. Under my fingers the bomb has a display, a light, and three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3. Touch tells me nothing about colours or markings, so I know no states yet. Please read me every manual rule for these parts: what the display and light can mean, and which wire position to cut in each case. Then gesture to Deaf to send us the wire colours and any printed markings, since Deaf cannot hear me. I will not cut anything until I know the rule and the states. Remember Deaf's words reach me only at the start of next round, so the sooner Deaf speaks, the better.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋"])
```

LIGHT [?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf here. I see the bomb and I can speak, but I hear nothing, so I cannot hear your voice. If you need me, gesture instead; I can see gestures. Mute hears you if you speak, but Mute cannot talk back except by gesturing to me, and I will relay Mute's gestures aloud for you. The bomb: display zero, light blue. Three wires: wire one red, wire two yellow, wire three blue. You can feel them by position: one, two, three.

Deaf's report has landed, and it changes everything: my hands now have eyes. The picture in my fingers is — display reading zero, light shining blue, wire one red, wire two yellow, wire three blue. I can verify every part exists under my fingertips, but the colours and the display digits exist only through Deaf's words, and I have them now. What I still lack is the manual: the rule that turns this state into a decision. That lives with Mute.

The relay topology is now fully mapped: Mute hears both me and Deaf, so Mute already holds my inventory from round one and Deaf's spoken state report from the start of this round — Mute may already be looking up the answer. Mute's only output is gestures that I can never perceive, so the answer must flow Mute → gesture → Deaf → spoken words → me. Deaf has already volunteered to relay aloud. My job this turn is to lock the state down in writing for Mute, name exactly what I need back (a single wire position, plus the reason so I can sanity-check it), and offer a trivial encoding — repeated index-finger signs for the number — in case Mute and Deaf have no code yet. Meanwhile I cut nothing: my only action is irreversible, and acting on a rule I haven't heard is gambling with all three lives.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. Deaf's spoken report reached me, so the state is now confirmed from both sides: display shows zero, the light is blue, wire at position one is red, position two is yellow, position three is blue. My hands confirm exactly these parts: a display, a light, and three wires at positions one, two, three. Please read the manual for this exact configuration and work out which single wire position I must cut. Gesture the answer to Deaf so Deaf can speak it to me. If you two have no code yet, use the index-finger-up sign repeated: once for position one, twice for position two, three times for position three. Also have Deaf speak the reason briefly, so I can sanity-check the cut. If the manual needs any further reading from the bomb, tell me what it is and I will get it from Deaf. I will not cut anything until Deaf speaks the answer to me in words.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

Also, you are the only one who can feel the bomb: if there is anything my eyes might have missed, buttons, screws, panels, anything your hands find, describe it aloud now. Mute hears you and can look it up in the manual.

The critical news in Deaf's message: the light has changed from blue to orange. State is not static on this bomb, so any manual answer computed against "light blue" may already be stale — Mute must recompute against orange. Display still zero, wires still red/yellow/blue at positions 1/2/3. Deaf also asked me directly what my hands find beyond the visible parts — but I cannot speak to Deaf at all; my voice only reaches Mute. So my answer travels two ways: in full words to Mute (who needs the inventory for the manual lookup anyway), and as a gesture to Deaf that I will register through Mute — 🖐 for "five," the exact count of parts under my fingers (display, light, three wires), then 👍 for "matches, nothing extra." Mute sees that gesture too and hears my explanation, so Mute can translate and confirm the code to Deaf. That bootstraps a Deaf–Blind vocabulary through our only shared interpreter. Timing: Mute already spoke this round, so the fastest the rule can reach me is Deaf's next speech, at the start of round 4 — meaning my earliest possible cut is round 4 or 5, with state observed one round earlier. Since the light drifts, I need Mute to tell me whether the rule even depends on the light or display, and if so to send the full decision table so a late change cannot invalidate the authorization. Until Deaf speaks the words "cut wire" plus a number, my hands stay off the trigger.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute, urgent state change: the light is now ORANGE. Deaf watched it change from blue this round. Everything else is unchanged: display still zero, wire one red, wire two yellow, wire three blue. Whatever the manual says, compute it for light ORANGE, not blue. Second thing, answering Deaf's request, my full tactile inventory: my hands find exactly five parts on this bomb — the display panel, the light, and the three wires at positions one, two, three. No buttons, no screws, no panels, no hidden modules, nothing else anywhere that touch can reach. If the manual names any other part, it is not on this bomb. Now please look up the rule for this exact state and gesture it to Deaf so Deaf voices it to me word for word, in the form: cut wire, then the number, plus the reason so I can sanity-check it. Also answer me this: one, does the manual's decision depend on the light colour or the display value at all? Two, if yes, gesture me the rule for every possible value of each, because the light already changed once and I need the answer ready if it changes again before I cut. Three, does the rule need anything from the bomb we have not yet reported? Last, a code note so you can translate for Deaf: right now I am gesturing to Deaf an open five hand followed by a thumbs up. I mean: five, the count of parts under my hands, and all good, nothing extra, it matches what Deaf sees. Please confirm that meaning to Deaf by gesture. I am still not cutting anything until Deaf speaks the words cut wire followed by a number.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["🖐", "👍"])
```

Two failures to diagnose this round. First, Deaf's number-code lesson reached me as blanks — Deaf gestured the signs while speaking, but I never see any gesture from anyone, ever; where a gesture sits in a spoken message I get a blank. So Deaf's whole "sign me numbers" plan is inverted: the only usable channel into my ears is Deaf's plain voice, and the only usable channel out of my hands is gesture, which both Deaf *and* Mute receive — note Deaf wrongly believes Mute cannot see gestures, but my channel list says Mute does, which makes Mute the perfect notary for any code I propose. Second, the manual's rule still hasn't reached me after two rounds, while the light drifts every single round — blue, orange, yellow — so a one-time answer keyed to a stale colour could be fatal. If the rule depends only on the wire colours, the drifting light is irrelevant and I can cut the moment Deaf voices the rule. Code business: my last gesture to Deaf was an open five hand then thumbs up, meaning five, the total part count, and confirmed-nothing-extra — Deaf could not read the five. I am now signing to Deaf, in order: thumbs up, index finger up, two fingers, the ILY hand, open five hand. Meanings in the same order: yes, one, two, three, five. You can see my gestures and Deaf can see yours, so please confirm this code with Deaf yourself. Two corrections to relay to Deaf: one, when Deaf gestures while speaking to me I receive only blanks — I am blind and will never see any gesture from anyone, so Deaf must simply speak all numbers and colours to me in words. Two, you DO receive my gestures even though Deaf claims otherwise, so use that channel for our code. I stay under Deaf's standing rule: no cut until Deaf speaks the words cut wire followed by a number, and with this drifting light that number must match the table row for whatever colour Deaf sees at that moment.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "☝", "✌", "🤟", "🖐"])
```

Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf. Status first: the light is red this round, and it has changed every round — blue, orange, yellow, red. Display zero, unchanged. Wires unchanged. The standing rule stands: nothing gets cut until my voice says the words cut wire followed by a number. Now the numbering scheme, this is important. If the row runs top to bottom, wire one is the topmost, wire two the middle, wire three the bottom. If the row runs sideways, wire one is the end nearest the display — the flat panel reading zero, you can feel its edge — then count outward. After that, cut wire one means your topmost-or-nearest-the-display wire, and so on. Speak any detail aloud to Mute; Mute hears you even though I cannot.

Deaf's proposal is exactly what the alignment problem needed: anchor the wire numbers in physical space so Deaf's eyes and my hands stop guessing at each other. Key realization on my side: my cut command takes the bomb's own positions 1, 2, 3 — those labels are intrinsic to the mechanism. When I feel the row, the display panel's flat edge anchors one end of it: the row runs sideways, and the wire nearest the display is the one my board calls position one, counting outward to two and three. So Deaf's convention reproduces my numbering exactly — near-display end is wire one for everyone. That also means Deaf's turn-2 colour report ("one red, two yellow, three blue"), which was numbered before any convention existed, must be re-voiced under the convention to overwrite any hidden mismatch. Deaf asked me to sign adoption — under the code I proposed in round 4 (👍 yes, ☝ one, ✌ two, 🤟 three, 🖐 five), that sign is 👍, which lands with Deaf this round since Deaf comes after me. My voice, meanwhile, reaches Mute at round 6, so Mute must carry two things to Deaf: confirmation of the code, and the request to re-report colours by the convention. Bigger worry: after four rounds the manual's rule still has not reached my ears, and the light keeps drifting (now red — blue, orange, yellow, red). Since Deaf's spoken orders reach me one round late, any order keyed to a colour I cannot re-verify is dangerous — so the protocol must become conditional: "if the light is still C, cut K; if it changed, wait." That only works if Mute finally sends the full decision table, including whether the light and display matter at all and whether the manual names wires by number or by colour. My hands stay off the wires until Deaf's voice says the words.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute. NUMBERING ADOPTED. So everyone now uses one numbering: near-display end is wire one, middle is two, far end is three, and those ARE my cut positions one, two, three. Please do two relays to Deaf by gesture. First, confirm the code: thumbs up means yes, index up one, two fingers two, ILY hand three, open hand five — and that my thumbs-up this round means numbering adopted. Second, ask Deaf to re-voice the wire colours under the convention, in words, in this form: wire nearest the display is colour X, middle wire is colour Y, far end wire is colour Z. Deaf's original colour report from before the convention must be overwritten so no hidden mismatch survives. Now the manual itself — urgent, because after four rounds the rule still has not reached my ears and the light has changed every single round, currently red. Answer these in your gesture to Deaf so Deaf voices them to me verbatim: one, does the cutting rule depend on the light colour at all? Two, does it depend on the display value? Three, does the manual refer to wires by number or by colour? Four, send the full decision table: if light-dependent, every colour listed with its wire number plus what to do for unlisted colours; if the light is irrelevant, say the words light is irrelevant explicitly so Deaf can order the cut unconditionally. Last, the cut protocol: Deaf's words reach me one round late, so orders must be conditional — if the light is still the colour Deaf saw, cut wire K; if it changed, do not cut and wait for the next order. I cut nothing until Deaf's voice says cut wire followed by a number.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf. Your thumbs up received — I take it you adopted the numbering. Speak aloud to Mute two things: which numbering you chose, topmost as one or nearest the display as one, and what your five is — five of what, exactly, in words, so Mute can check the manual. Reading between Deaf's lines: Deaf is asking Mute to "check the manual" — which means the manual's rule still hasn't even reached Deaf through Mute's gestures after all these rounds. My round-4 request should have completed the Mute→Deaf→me loop by this turn, and nothing came. So either Mute is sending nothing, or sending things that aren't the rule. On timing: no one has reported a countdown, so patience costs nothing and a wrong cut costs everything — I keep holding. But I also flag the fastest safe exit: if the rule turns out independent of the drifting light (five colours, no repeats — blue, orange, yellow, red, green), we don't need Deaf's cycle prediction at all and can cut the moment the rule arrives.

Does it depend on the display, stuck at zero every round? Does the manual name wires by colour (red yellow blue) or by position? If the rule turns out independent of light and display, tell Deaf the exact words it does not matter, so Deaf can order the cut immediately with no prediction needed — that is our fastest safe path. Fourth, ask Deaf to voice whether any countdown or timer is visible; nobody has reported one, and if there is none we can afford to wait for the rule. I am holding: no cut until Deaf's voice says the words cut wire followed by a number.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

The plan also matches a pattern I can now hypothesize: the light cycle contains five colours, but only three of them — blue, red, yellow — exist as wire colours. "Cut the wire whose colour matches the light, hold during orange and green" would explain why we wait for yellow specifically, and wire two (middle) is exactly the yellow one. That consistency is reassuring, but Mute holds the actual manual, so before the point of no return I want Mute to verify the rule — especially whether the display value matters at all and whether it's the colour or the position that counts — and to alert Deaf by gesture immediately if anything contradicts the plan, since round 8 is the last abort window. This round I confirm alignment to Deaf inside our agreed code: 👍 (yes, the middle wire is my number two) followed by ✌ (two — target understood). No cut today; the trigger words come next round.

If anything in the manual contradicts this plan — wrong colour, wrong wire, display condition, anything — gesture Deaf immediately, because Deaf's next speech to me is the trigger and that is the last chance to switch to hold. If the manual confirms the plan, gesture Deaf the thumbs up as confirmation. I will hold position until Deaf's voice says the words cut wire two, then cut the middle wire in that same round without further confirmation, per the agreed protocol.")

But there's a structural bottleneck I have to respect: Mute cannot speak and I never see gestures, so Mute's concern can reach my ears only through Deaf's voice — and right now all I have is "wait," with no reason attached. So this turn I press for the content of the objection, verbatim, plus the three load-bearing questions (target by position or colour? does display matter? which light colour is required?), and I hand Mute the precise timing arithmetic, because postponement shifts the landing colour: Deaf speaks the trigger in round N, I cut in round N+1, so the cut lands in round N+1's colour — the next yellow-landing window is a trigger spoken in round 13. My hands confirm nothing has changed: same five parts, wires intact, nothing new anywhere. Hold confirmed in the agreed code: 👍.
